title: Before You Begin: Your Azure Lab, Tools and Cost Guardrails (Basic)
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Explain how a lunch, its demo and its independent lab fit together, and plan your way through the two months of the course.
- Choose a safe subscription for learning (free account, Azure for Students or pay-as-you-go) and explain what a spending limit does and does not do.
- Compare the Azure portal, Azure Cloud Shell, the Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell, and describe how every request reaches Azure Resource Manager and a resource provider.
- Apply the course's lab conventions and cost guardrails: one region, one tagged resource group per lab, a budget with alerts, and a cleanup habit.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

It is your first Monday as the new cloud engineer at PT Nusantara Retail. Pak Budi, who runs head-office IT, gives you the tour. It ends in a small room next to the pantry: one physical server, a humming fan, and a UPS that beeps whenever the coffee machine starts. That server runs the online storefront for customers of all forty stores. Traffic has tripled this year. The server has not.

At last month's meeting Ibu Sari, the director, asked a simple question: "If that server dies, how long can't we sell?" Nobody answered.

She has given you time to learn Azure properly, with one condition: "No surprise bills. I want to be able to explain every rupiah." Before you design anything, you need a place to practise, the right tools, and guardrails that keep spending predictable.

Today's question: how do you set up an Azure lab where you can experiment freely, without risking the company or the budget?

Reading

1. How this course works

This course is built for people who learn in short, regular bursts. Each lunch is one hour you can protect in your calendar, and every lunch follows the same rhythm, so you always know where you are.

Minutes | Segment | What you do
5 | Scenario | Meet today's Nusantara Retail problem and the objectives.
25 | Reading | Learn the concepts in plain language, with diagrams and tables.
15 | Demo | Step through an interactive animation; optionally watch a short walkthrough video.
5 | Knowledge check | Answer five scenario questions. Each answer explains why.
5 | Takeaways | Review the five key points and preview the lab.
5 | Buffer | Finish your lunch. Really.

The hands-on lab is deliberately not part of the hour. Most labs take 30 to 90 minutes (the capstones longer), sometimes with waiting time, so you do them later: in the evening, at the weekend, whenever suits you. Every lab is independent. It creates everything it needs, so you can do Lab 17 without ever touching Labs 1 to 16. When a lab needs a starting point, such as two web servers for the load-balancing lab, a setup.sh script builds it for you. Every lab that creates Azure resources also ships a verify.sh that checks your work and a cleanup.sh that removes everything again.

Labs come in two modes. Guided mode explains every step. Challenge mode gives you the requirements only: build it your way, then let verify.sh judge the result.

The course runs over two "months" of weekday lunches:

The core month (Lunches 01–21) covers every fundamental service at the level you need to explain it, choose it and use it. It follows the skills measured for the AZ-900 Azure Fundamentals exam and ends with a capstone that pulls everything together. The deep-dive month (Lunches 22–31) returns to the big topics, such as identity, virtual machines, networking, databases and governance, at the depth an administrator or architect needs. A topic that does not fit into one hour is split into a Basic lunch and an Advanced partner: Lunch 06 (Virtual Machines, Basic) pairs with Lunch 23 (Virtual Machines, Advanced), for example.

Every lab shows a cost band in its header, so you know what to expect before you start:

Band | Meaning | Typical labs
| Free or close to free | resource groups, storage, policies, this lab
| Small charges while resources run, typically cents per hour | virtual machines, load balancers, monitoring
| Noticeable charges while running, or slow-to-create gateways | VPN gateways, Application Gateway, AKS — delete them straight away

The course never quotes exact prices, because prices change and differ by region. When you want numbers, the Azure pricing calculator gives you current ones; you will use it in Lab 02.

2. Meet Nusantara Retail

Every lunch moves one company a step closer to answering the director's question. PT Nusantara Retail is a mid-sized retailer with forty stores across Indonesia and a head office in Jakarta. Its e-commerce site, which everyone calls the storefront, runs on that single server by the pantry. If the server fails, online sales stop until someone fixes it.

You will meet the same people again and again:

Person | Role | What they care about
Ibu Sari | Director | Risk and cost. She wants answers in rupiah and in hours of downtime.
Dewi | Developer | Shipping features fast, without waiting weeks for a server.
Pak Budi | Head-office IT | The on-premises network (10.0.0.0/16) and everything plugged into it. Careful with change.
Rizky | Outsourced contractor | Getting just enough access to do his job, and no more.
The finance team | Budget owners | Monthly bills that match what was approved.
You | New cloud engineer | Turning all of the above into a working Azure design.

One fact shapes many later decisions: Nusantara Retail wants its customer data to stay in Indonesia. In production, the storefront would therefore run in the Indonesia Central region in Jakarta. The labs default to Southeast Asia (Singapore) because it offers the broadest choice of services. Lunch 03 explains regions properly and shows you how to choose.

3. A subscription you can safely break

To create anything in Azure you need a subscription: a billing and management container that your resources live in. You sign in with an account (a Microsoft account, a GitHub account or a work account), and every subscription trusts one tenant, the Microsoft Entra ID directory that holds users and groups. Lunch 04 explores this hierarchy. For now, remember two things: resources live in subscriptions, and every subscription has someone paying for it.

For this course you want a subscription that is yours alone. There are three common ways to get one:

Option | What you get (always check the current offer) | Card needed? | Good to know
Azure free account | US$200 credit for the first 30 days; popular services free for 12 months (for example 750 hours a month of a small B-series VM); 65+ always-free services | Yes, for identity verification | Spending limit on by default. To continue after 30 days, or once the credit is used, you move to pay-as-you-go. The 12-month free services are for new customers who make that move within 30 days.
Azure for Students | US$100 credit to use within 12 months, plus free services | No; you verify with your academic email | For students at eligible institutions; you can renew every year while you study.
Pay-as-you-go | No credit; free monthly amounts of selected services; you pay for usage beyond them | Yes | No spending limit. Budgets and your cleanup habit are your only brakes.

Read the Azure account options page and the Azure for Students page before you sign up, because offers change.

The spending limit. Credit-based subscriptions, including the free account, come with a spending limit switched on. It is not a number you pick: it equals your credit, and you cannot raise or lower it. You can only keep it or remove it. When your usage exhausts the credit, Azure disables your resources for the rest of the billing period: virtual machines are stopped and deallocated, and storage becomes read-only. Covered services stop costing you money, but they also stop running. The limit has gaps, too: some Azure Marketplace products and support plans are billed separately. And it disappears completely when you move a free account to pay-as-you-go. Pay-as-you-go subscriptions cannot have a spending limit at all.

Which one should you pick? If you are a student, start with Azure for Students. Otherwise, a free account is a comfortable start: the first lunches cost little, and the credit absorbs mistakes. When the 30 days end, you can move to pay-as-you-go and keep the same subscription. Do one thing before that move: create the budget from Lab 01, because the safety net of the spending limit goes away at the same moment. If you have a Visual Studio subscription, it may include a monthly Azure credit for development and testing; check your subscriber benefits. Not sure what you already have? In the portal, open Subscriptions, select the subscription, and look at its offer on the Overview page.

Warning: Never do these labs in a company or production subscription, not even "just for a quick test". Your experiments can break shared resources, your costs land on someone else's budget, company policies may block lab steps, and cleanup scripts delete whole resource groups. Use a personal subscription, or one your employer created only for your learning.

Protect the account. An account that can create resources can also create bills. Microsoft now requires multifactor authentication (MFA) for Azure sign-ins: first for the portal, and since 2025 also for the Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell and infrastructure-as-code tools whenever they create, change or delete resources. Set up the Microsoft Authenticator app or a passkey when you are prompted, never share your sign-in, and never commit keys or passwords to Git.

4. Three ways in, one front door

You can manage Azure from a web page, from a terminal in your browser, or from your own computer. The four tools below all do the same job; they suit different moments.

Tool | What it is | Best for | Setup
Azure portal | The web interface at portal.azure.com | Exploring, visual views (costs, metrics, diagrams), one-off tasks | None; sign in with a browser
Azure Cloud Shell | A browser-based terminal running Bash or PowerShell, already signed in | Every lab in this course; quick scripts from any computer | None; open it from the portal toolbar or at shell.azure.com
Azure CLI (az) | A cross-platform command-line tool | Repeatable scripts, Bash users, automation | Install on Windows, macOS or Linux, then az login
Azure PowerShell (Az module) | PowerShell cmdlets such as New-AzResourceGroup | Windows administrators, PowerShell pipelines | Install the Az module (PowerShell 7 recommended), then Connect-AzAccount

Azure Cloud Shell deserves a closer look, because every lab uses it. It runs on a temporary Linux host that Microsoft manages, with the Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, Bicep, Git and many other tools already installed. A session times out after 20 minutes without keyboard activity. The first time you open it, you choose how to treat your files:

- An ephemeral session needs no storage account. It starts fastest, but everything you saved is deleted when the session ends.
- Persistent storage mounts an Azure Files share from a storage account in your subscription. Your $HOME directory survives between sessions, and so do your copy of the course repository and your lab suffix. The storage account costs a little, like any storage.

For this course, persistent storage saves you from cloning the repository again every time, but either choice works.

On your own computer, Visual Studio Code with the Bicep, Azure Resources and Azure CLI Tools extensions becomes a comfortable Azure workbench. Lab 01 lists the local tools as optional extras; you never need them for the labs.

What happens when you click Create. Whichever tool you use, the request goes to the same place: Azure Resource Manager (ARM), the deployment and management service for Azure. ARM checks who you are, using a token from Microsoft Entra ID. It checks that you are allowed to perform the action, using Azure role-based access control. It validates the request: is that region name real, does a policy forbid this? Only then does it hand the request to the right resource provider, the service that knows how to build that type of resource, such as Microsoft.Compute for virtual machines or Microsoft.Storage for storage accounts.

Because every tool talks to the same API, a click and a command give the same result. That is why the labs can show a CLI command and a portal path for the same task, and why anything you can click, you can also script.

Which tool when? At Nusantara Retail, the finance team will live in the portal's Cost Management views, because charts beat commands for spotting a trend. Dewi will script her deployments with the Azure CLI, so they can be reviewed and repeated. Pak Budi already has PowerShell scripts for his Windows servers and will feel at home with Azure PowerShell. This course teaches CLI first, because commands are easy to copy, compare and re-run, and it shows the portal path whenever the portal teaches something visual.

One more term you will meet early: a subscription must be registered for a resource provider before it can use that provider's resource types. The portal, and deployments of templates, usually register the common providers for you the first time you need them. If you ever see an error saying a subscription is not registered to use a namespace (for example Microsoft.CloudShell the first time you open Cloud Shell), open Subscriptions › your subscription › Resource providers, find the namespace and select Register.

5. Lab conventions and cost guardrails

A few conventions keep the labs predictable, cheap and easy to clean up. They live in labs/common/config.sh, which every lab script loads first.

- One region. LOCATION defaults to southeastasia. Learners in Indonesia can use indonesiacentral instead: run export LOCATION=indonesiacentral before source ../common/config.sh, and check that each lab's services are offered there.
- One resource group per lab. A resource group is a container for related resources. Lab NN works in rg-lunchNN-<suffix>, so deleting that single group deletes everything the lab created.
- Tags. Every lab resource group carries two tags, which are name-value labels: course=azure-fundamentals-lunches and lunch=NN. Cleanup scripts and check-environment.sh find leftovers by these tags.
- Names. Resources follow the Cloud Adoption Framework abbreviations (vnet- for virtual networks, vm- for virtual machines, st for storage accounts) plus a random suffix of five lowercase letters and digits. Some names, such as those of storage accounts and web apps, must be globally unique; the suffix prevents clashes with other learners. It is generated once and kept in ~/.azlunches-suffix.
- Small sizes. Labs use small, burstable VM sizes and stay at or below four vCPUs at a time, because free and trial subscriptions have small quotas.

Now the guardrails, the habits that keep Ibu Sari's "no surprise bills" promise:

1. A budget with alerts. In Cost Management, a budget tracks spending against an amount you choose for a month, quarter or year. You attach alerts at percentages of that amount. This course uses 50%, 80% and 100% of actual cost, and Azure emails you as spending crosses each one. A forecasted alert can warn you earlier, when Azure predicts that you will cross a threshold.
2. The spending limit, if your subscription has one, as the last line of defence.
3. Cost bands and small default sizes, so you know what a lab costs before you start.
4. Auto-shutdown on lab VMs, so a forgotten VM switches itself off at night. You configure it in Lunch 06.
5. The cleanup habit. Run bash cleanup.sh on the day you finish a lab. Once a week, run bash labs/common/check-environment.sh; it lists any course resource groups that are still alive. Cleanup scripts also remove what lives outside a resource group, such as role assignments, policy assignments or test users, so always prefer them to deleting the group by hand.

Here is how the guardrails play out in a typical month. You finish the virtual machine lab on a Friday evening but forget to run the cleanup script. On Sunday the 50% email arrives. On Monday you run check-environment.sh, which lists rg-lunch06-<suffix> as still alive, and one cleanup.sh later the meter stops. Without the budget, you would have discovered the VM on your invoice weeks later.

Tip: Budget alerts come from azure-noreply@microsoft.com. Add that address to your safe senders list today, so the one email that matters does not end up in your junk folder.

Important: A budget is an alarm, not a brake. Crossing 100% sends an email; it does not stop or delete anything. Cost data also takes time to arrive (often 8 to 24 hours, sometimes longer) and budgets are evaluated about once a day, so an alert can arrive many hours after the spending happened. The only things that actually stop spending are the spending limit on credit-based subscriptions, and you, deleting resources.

6. How it fits together for Nusantara Retail

Picture the pantry room again. Before you touch the storefront, you now have a safe sandbox: a personal or dedicated subscription, protected by MFA, that holds nothing the company depends on. If it is a free account, the spending limit caps the damage at the credit. A monthly budget with alerts at 50%, 80% and 100% gives you early warnings, and a forecast alert warns you even earlier.

You also have a way of working that suits everyone around you. Ibu Sari gets predictability: labs are tagged, grouped, costed in bands and cleaned up on the same day. Dewi gets speed: Cloud Shell is ready in seconds in any browser, with nothing to install. Pak Budi gets reassurance: nothing in your lab touches his 10.0.0.0/16 network or the company's subscriptions. And when Rizky the contractor arrives in Lunch 05, you will already know that every request, his included, passes through Azure Resource Manager, where identity and permissions are checked.

The director's question is still open. To answer it, you first need the vocabulary of the cloud: what you rent, what you still own, and why paying only for what you use changes the economics of that single server. That is Lunch 02.

Pause and think: your free account has a spending limit, and you have also created a monthly budget with a 100% alert. Spending reaches both on the same day. Which one stops your virtual machines, and which one only sends an email? What changes on the day you move the subscription to pay-as-you-go?

Field notes from Stefanus

Write the delete command first. Before I build anything in Azure, even a five-minute test, I write down the command that will remove it. In this course that line is bash cleanup.sh; in my own work it is usually one az group delete, plus a note for anything that lives outside the group, such as a role assignment. If I cannot write that line, I am about to scatter resources that I will later have to hunt for. My second habit takes five seconds: I run az account show before the first command of every session. A typo fails loudly, as you will see in Lab 01; a perfectly correct command in the wrong subscription succeeds quietly. So give your lab subscription a name you cannot mistake. A budget email reminds me of what I forgot, a day late; the delete line works tonight.

Go further

- What is Azure Cloud Shell? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/cloud-shell/overview) — the shell you will use in every lab: tools, session time-outs and storage options.
- Azure spending limit (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/cost-management-billing/manage/spending-limit) — which subscriptions have one, what it blocks, and how to remove it or turn it back on.
- Tutorial: Create and manage budgets (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/cost-management-billing/costs/tutorial-acm-create-budgets) — every budget option, including forecasted alerts and action groups.
- What is Azure Resource Manager? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-resource-manager/management/overview) — the front door every request passes through, and the terms you will meet again in Lunch 04.

quiz.q: Dewi says: "I'll just try the labs in the company's production subscription. I'll delete everything afterwards." What do you tell her?
quiz.a: Use a personal or dedicated lab subscription instead. Why: lab steps and cleanup scripts can break or delete shared resources, the costs land on someone else's budget, and company policies may block lab steps.

quiz.q: You created a monthly budget with alerts at 50%, 80% and 100%. You forget a VM, and actual spending reaches 130% of the budget before you notice. What happened to the VM?
quiz.a: Nothing: it is still running and still costing money. Why: budgets only send notifications; they never stop or delete resources.

quiz.q: On day 20 your free-account credit runs out and you have not moved to pay-as-you-go. What happens to your virtual machine and your storage account?
quiz.a: The spending limit disables them: the VM is stopped and deallocated, and the storage account becomes read-only. To continue, you move to pay-as-you-go, which removes the limit. Why: the spending limit equals the credit and is designed to stop spending rather than bill you.

quiz.q: Pak Budi creates a storage account in the portal. Dewi creates another with az storage account create. Which service receives and checks both requests, and which one actually builds the storage accounts?
quiz.a: Azure Resource Manager receives, authenticates, authorizes and validates both requests; the Microsoft.Storage resource provider builds the accounts. Why: every Azure tool calls the same Resource Manager API.

quiz.q: Yesterday you cloned the course repository in Cloud Shell. Today the folder is gone and config.sh has generated a new suffix. What happened, and how do you prevent it?
quiz.a: You were using an ephemeral session, whose files are deleted when it ends. Switch to persistent storage (Cloud Shell Settings › Reset user settings, then mount a storage account), or write your suffix down and restore it with echo <suffix> > ~/.azlunches-suffix after cloning again. Why: only persistent storage keeps $HOME between sessions.

takeaways: A lunch is one hour of scenario, reading, demo and quiz. Labs are independent, done later at your own pace, and always end with verify.sh and cleanup.sh.
Learn in a personal or dedicated lab subscription protected by MFA, never in a company or production subscription.

A spending limit (free account and other credit-based offers) disables resources when the credit is gone; a budget only sends alerts. Pay-as-you-go has no spending limit, so your budget and cleanup habit matter even more there.

The portal, Cloud Shell, the Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell all send requests to Azure Resource Manager, which checks them and hands them to resource providers. The labs use Bash and the Azure CLI in Cloud Shell.
One region, one tagged resource group per lab and a random suffix make cleanup a single command: deleting the group deletes everything inside it.

lab.title: Set up your lab environment
lab.text:
What you'll build

By the end of this lab your subscription is ready for the whole course. Cloud Shell works, the course files are in your home directory, the environment check passes, and a monthly budget with alerts at 50%, 80% and 100% watches over everything you will build in the next thirty lunches. You also rehearse the rhythm Nusantara Retail's new cloud engineer will follow in every lab — create a tagged resource group, inspect it, delete it — and you learn to read an Azure error message.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you can create resources and that is not a company or production subscription. No subscription yet? Section 3 of the Lunch 01 reading (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/lunches/01-before-you-begin.html#3-a-subscription-you-can-safely-break) compares the free account, Azure for Students and pay-as-you-go.
- The Owner or Contributor role on that subscription. If you created the subscription yourself, you are Owner. Creating a budget needs at least Contributor.
- A web browser. Nothing to install: this lab runs in Azure Cloud Shell.

Important: This lab creates only a resource group and a budget, and both are free. Finish with the Clean up section anyway: the habit matters more than the money today.

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–5 below (Task 6 is optional)
Challenge | you already know the basics | read only the Challenge brief, do it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · Open Cloud Shell and get the course files

Cloud Shell is the workbench for every lab: it is already signed in and has the Azure CLI, Git and Bicep installed.

1. Sign in to the Azure portal with your lab account and complete the MFA prompt.
2. Select the Cloud Shell icon (>_) in the top toolbar, or open shell.azure.com in a new browser tab for a full-size terminal.
3. The first time, choose Bash. In the Getting started pane, choose a storage option:
  - Mount storage account › We will create a storage account for you — recommended for this course. Your files and your lab suffix survive between sessions. The storage account costs a little, like any storage.
  - No storage account required — an ephemeral session. It is free and fast, but every file is deleted when the session ends.
  Select your lab subscription in the drop-down and confirm.
4. Check which subscription the CLI is using:
  az account show --query "{subscription:name, state:state, user:user.name}" --output table

  If you have more than one subscription, list them and switch to your lab subscription:
  az account list --query "[].{name:name, id:id, state:state}" --output table
  az account set --subscription "<your lab subscription name or ID>"

5. Clone the course repository and run the environment check:
  cd ~
  git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
  cd azure-fundamentals-lunches
  bash labs/common/check-environment.sh

  The check only reads information; it creates nothing. It confirms that the CLI is signed in and your subscription is enabled, that the default region exists, and that the small VM sizes used by the labs are available to you. It also shows your regional vCPU quota and lists any lab resource groups you forgot to delete. The VM-size check takes about 30 seconds.

Tip: Using ephemeral sessions? Your clone and your lab suffix disappear when the session ends. Note the suffix now with cat ~/.azlunches-suffix. Next time, after cloning again, restore it with echo <your-suffix> > ~/.azlunches-suffix so later scripts find the resources you created. To switch to persistent storage, open Cloud Shell Settings › Reset user settings and choose Mount storage account at the next start.

Checkpoint: az account show reports Enabled, and check-environment.sh ends with All N checks passed. Nice work! If only a VM-size check fails, your setup is still fine for this lab; the VM labs explain how to choose another size.

Task 2 · Create a monthly budget with alerts (portal)

The budget is the guardrail for the whole course. You create it once and keep it: every lab's spending counts against it. Budgets are easiest to create in the portal.

1. In the portal search bar, type Cost Management and open it. In the left menu, select Budgets. (Another route: Subscriptions › your lab subscription › Budgets.)
2. Check the Scope shown at the top. It must be your lab subscription, not a resource group or a management group. Select the scope to change it if needed.
3. Select + Add and fill in Create a budget:
  - Name: budget-azure-lunches
  - Reset period: Monthly. (If your subscription also offers Billing month, that one follows your invoice dates; either is fine.)
  - Creation date: keep the default, the current month.
  - Expiration date: at least a year from now. When a budget expires, Azure deletes it.
  - Amount: what you are willing to spend on learning in one month, in your billing currency, for example the equivalent of US$20. The chart on the page helps you choose; there is no wrong answer.
4. Select Next. Under Alert conditions, add three rows with Type set to Actual and % of budget set to 50, 80 and 100. Optionally add a fourth row: Type Forecasted, 100.
5. Under Alert recipients (email), enter your own e-mail address (you can add up to five). Choose your language and select Create.

You can also look at budgets from Cloud Shell. The consumption command group is in preview, so a warning line about that is normal:

az consumption budget list --query "[].{name:name, amount:amount, period:timeGrain}" --output table

If budgets are not available to you. Some subscription types, for example Azure for Students, Azure for Students Starter and sponsorship offers, are listed as not supported by Cost Management. Separately, a brand-new subscription can take up to 48 hours before every Cost Management feature appears. If the Budgets page shows an error or no Add button:

- if your subscription is only a day or two old, try again tomorrow;
- otherwise, use the fallback guardrails: keep your subscription's spending limit switched on (credit-based offers have it by default), check your usage every week (Azure for Students: the Education page in the portal shows your usage), and run check-environment.sh weekly to catch leftovers. verify.sh recognises these offers and checks the spending limit instead of a budget.

Checkpoint: Cost Management › Budgets lists budget-azure-lunches with your amount and a monthly reset period. The CLI command above shows it too; a new budget can take a few minutes to appear there.

Task 3 · Create a tagged resource group with the CLI

Every lab keeps its resources in one tagged resource group. Practising on an empty group costs nothing.

cd ~/azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/01-before-you-begin
source ../common/config.sh
RG=$(rg_name 01)
echo "$RG"

config.sh prints the lab settings (region, suffix, VM sizes). rg_name 01 builds the name of this lab's group, for example rg-lunch01-ab12c. Create the group with the shared helper:

ensure_rg "$RG" 01

ensure_rg is a small function in labs/common/helpers.sh. It runs exactly this plain Azure CLI command, which you could type instead (running both is harmless; the second one simply updates the same group):

az group create \
  --name "$RG" \
  --location "$LOCATION" \
  --tags course="$COURSE_TAG" lunch=01 \
  --output none

Now look at what you created:

az group show --name "$RG" \
  --query "{name:name, location:location, tags:tags, state:properties.provisioningState}" --output json
az group list --tag course="$COURSE_TAG" --output table
az group show --name "$RG" --query id --output tsv

The last command prints the group's resource ID, its full address in Azure: /subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/<name>. Lunch 04 takes resource IDs apart.

Checkpoint: az group show reports "state": "Succeeded", the location from config.sh and both tags: course: azure-fundamentals-lunches and lunch: 01.

Task 4 · Find it in the portal

The portal and the CLI are two windows onto the same Azure Resource Manager. Whatever one creates, the other sees.

1. In the portal search bar, type Resource groups and open rg-lunch01-<suffix>. Refresh the list if it is not there yet.
2. Overview: the location and the two tags. The group is empty.
3. Tags (left menu): both tags are listed. Leave them as they are.
4. Activity log (left menu): an entry for the write operation on the resource group, with your account as the caller. Activity log entries can take a few minutes to appear.
5. JSON View (top right of the Overview page): the same resource ID you printed in Task 3, plus the tags.

Checkpoint: the portal shows the same name, location and tags as az group show, and the Activity log names your account as the caller.

Task 5 · Delete it

Cleanup is a habit. Deleting a resource group deletes everything inside it; here that is nothing, so it is a safe rehearsal.

az group delete --name "$RG" --yes
az group exists --name "$RG"

az group delete waits until the group is gone, which takes a few seconds for an empty group. Later labs often add --no-wait so deletion continues in the background; the cleanup.sh scripts do exactly that.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Resource groups › rg-lunch01-<suffix> › Delete resource group › type the name to confirm › Delete. The portal makes you type the name because deletion cannot be undone.

Checkpoint: az group exists --name "$RG" prints false.

Task 6 (optional) · Install the tools on your own computer

Cloud Shell is all you need for this course. If you also want a local setup:

Tool | Install | Then
Azure CLI | Windows: winget install --exact --id Microsoft.AzureCLI · macOS: brew update && brew install azure-cli · Ubuntu or Debian: curl -sL https://aka.ms/InstallAzureCLIDeb | sudo bash | az login (or az login --use-device-code on a remote machine), then az account set --subscription "<lab subscription>"
Bicep | az bicep install (the CLI also installs Bicep automatically the first time you deploy a Bicep file) | az bicep version
Azure PowerShell | Install PowerShell 7, then Install-Module -Name Az -Repository PSGallery -Scope CurrentUser -Force | Connect-AzAccount
Visual Studio Code | Extensions Bicep (ms-azuretools.vscode-bicep), Azure Resources (ms-azuretools.vscode-azureresourcegroups) and Azure CLI Tools (ms-vscode.azurecli) | Sign in from the Azure view in the side bar

Break it and fix it

A misspelled region name is one of the most common first errors. Make one on purpose, back in Cloud Shell:

cd ~/azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/01-before-you-begin
source ../common/config.sh
az group create --name "$(rg_name 01 typo)" --location southeastasai \
  --tags course="$COURSE_TAG" lunch=01

Symptom: the command fails and nothing is created. Read the error from the top. The text in parentheses is the error code; the message explains what was wrong and, here, even lists the valid values:

(LocationNotAvailableForResourceGroup) The provided location 'southeastasai' is not available for resource group. List of available regions is 'eastasia,southeastasia,australiaeast,...'.
Code: LocationNotAvailableForResourceGroup
Message: The provided location 'southeastasai' is not available for resource group. List of available regions is '...'.

Hint: how to fix it

Azure Resource Manager rejected the request before any resource provider was involved, because the region name does not exist. List the exact names Azure accepts and filter them:

az account list-locations --query "[?metadata.regionType=='Physical'].name" --output tsv | sort | grep -i -E 'asia|indonesia'

Run the command again with the correct name, southeastasia (or simply "$LOCATION"), then delete the group you just created:

az group create --name "$(rg_name 01 typo)" --location "$LOCATION" \
  --tags course="$COURSE_TAG" lunch=01 --output none
az group delete --name "$(rg_name 01 typo)" --yes

The lesson: Azure errors are specific. The code (LocationNotAvailableForResourceGroup) is easy to search for, and the message often tells you the valid values.

Verify your work

bash verify.sh

verify.sh checks that you are signed in, that your subscription is enabled, that a subscription-scope budget exists with monthly alerts at 50%, 80% and 100% (or, for subscription types without budgets, that the spending limit is on), and that no Lab 01 resource group is left behind. Every check should say PASS. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit.

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

This deletes any resource group left over from this lab: groups tagged lunch=01, plus rg-lunch01-<suffix> and rg-lunch01-typo-<suffix> if they exist without tags. It keeps your budget on purpose: the budget is free and protects every lab in the course. Delete it only when you have finished the course (Cost Management › Budgets › select it › Delete).

If you chose persistent storage, Cloud Shell created a storage account for your home directory, usually in a resource group named cloud-shell-storage-<region>. It is not part of this lab. Keep it while you take the course: deleting it erases your Cloud Shell files.

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
Cloud Shell does not start and mentions the Microsoft.CloudShell resource provider | The provider is not registered in this subscription | Portal › Subscriptions › your subscription › Resource providers › search cloudshell › Register, then reopen Cloud Shell
You are not signed in to Azure. Run: az login (printed by a lab script) | You are running locally and are not signed in, or your sign-in expired | Run az login, or use Cloud Shell
The Azure CLI was not found. | You are running a script on a computer without the Azure CLI | Use Cloud Shell, or install the CLI (Task 6)
check-environment.sh says a VM size is not available | That size is not offered to your subscription in your region | Fine for this lab. The VM labs explain how to set VM_SIZE and VM_SIZE_SMALL
The Budgets page shows an error or has no Add button | Brand-new subscription (up to 48 hours), or an offer that Cost Management does not support (for example Azure for Students or sponsorships) | Wait a day; otherwise use the fallback in Task 2
az consumption budget list returns nothing right after you created a budget | It can take a few minutes to appear, or the CLI is using another subscription | Wait, then check az account show
(AuthorizationFailed) The client ... does not have authorization to perform action 'Microsoft.Resources/subscriptions/resourcegroups/write' | Your account has only Reader access to the subscription | Use a subscription where you are Owner or Contributor
An error about MFA or a claims challenge when you create or delete something from the CLI | Mandatory MFA for create, update and delete operations | Run az login again and complete MFA; update an old CLI with az upgrade
Your cloned folder and ~/.azlunches-suffix have disappeared | You are using ephemeral sessions | Clone again and restore your suffix (see the tip in Task 1), or switch to persistent storage
(LocationNotAvailableForResourceGroup) The provided location '…' is not available for resource group. | A misspelled region name | See Break it and fix it

Stretch goals

- If you skipped it, add a Forecasted alert at 100% to your budget. Then add an action group that sends a push notification to the Azure mobile app.
- Try the same rhythm in Azure PowerShell: switch Cloud Shell to PowerShell and run New-AzResourceGroup -Name "rg-lunch01-ps-<suffix>" -Location southeastasia -Tag @{course="azure-fundamentals-lunches"; lunch="01"}, then Remove-AzResourceGroup -Name "rg-lunch01-ps-<suffix>" -Force. Same request, same Resource Manager, different syntax.
- Explore Cost Management › Cost analysis and change the view to Daily costs. Come back after a VM lab to see a real line appear.
- Run az group list --query "[].{name:name, location:location}" --output table and look for anything you did not create on purpose.

Challenge brief

Prepare your subscription for the course, any way you like (portal, CLI or PowerShell):

1. The Azure CLI is signed in (in Cloud Shell or locally) to a personal or dedicated lab subscription whose state is Enabled.
2. A monthly cost budget exists at subscription scope with actual-cost alerts at 50%, 80% and 100% sent to your e-mail address. (If your subscription type does not support budgets, its spending limit must be on.)
3. You created a resource group named rg-lunch01-<suffix> in your lab region, tagged course=azure-fundamentals-lunches and lunch=01, confirmed the tags in the portal, and then deleted it.
4. No resource group tagged lunch=01 remains.

Then run bash verify.sh. Stuck? solution.sh scripts the CLI parts, or switch to Guided mode.
